quotes.verbatim_quote:
All of the following 3-part chords are derived from the Major scale, the Melodic
Minor and the Harmonic Minor scales, but they are transposed to the root of C. (Twenty
3-part chords is perhaps misleading...3 close inversions plus 3 spread inversions for each
gives us one hundred twenty 3-part chords you should know...)
quotes.why_load_bearing: This defines the theoretical source of all 20 chord types in the chapter and corrects the misleading title by revealing the true scope of 120 voicings.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
As guitarists, we can see that 3-part chords are easier to play than 4-part chords.
Also, they often afford more space between the voices for melodic embellishment.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This gives the practical rationale for choosing 3-part chords, linking playability to the compositional advantage of space for melodic embellishment.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
If someone were to ask me: “Mr. Goodchord, what chapter in Volume III is the
most important?”, I would probably deny that there was such a thing... However,
if I was hooked-up to a lie-detector machine with a gun to my head I would surely reply:

“This chapter...”
quotes.why_load_bearing: The author explicitly singles out this chapter as the most important in the volume, signaling that mastery of these 20 structures is the central goal of the entire book.
